1.station: A slung horn at the summit. The line drops straight down the northeast face rather than following any rib or ridge, and the stations below are oddly rigged and scruffy rather than obvious — they come into view before you reach the end of a 60 m rope, not at it.
hazards: Easy to rappel past the next anchor: it appears short of the rope end and does not read as a station from above
Parties have had to free a jammed rappel rope on this descent, and one needed a handline thrown down to finish the exit gully
1.pull: Five single-rope rappels totalling roughly 400 ft, so a 60 m rope doubled covers every one — two ropes buy nothing here.

3.station: The third rappel ends at the start of a short, exposed grassy traverse running east to the next rock rib. The following anchor is on that rib, not beneath you, so you walk before you rappel again.
hazards: The link between the two anchors is a sloping grass-and-dirt traverse over slab with full exposure, and it is the section parties are usually unroped on

5.station: The last rappel lands on the East Ledges themselves. Some parties instead downclimb from the bottom of this rope to a further anchor on steep ledges above the Boston Glacier rather than walking straight off.
hazards: Several hundred metres of loose sandy and grassy 3rd-class ledges follow, with 4th-class steps where the ledges cross each rock rib
Cairns come in a higher and a lower set at every rib and the two are not equivalent — the low line finishes in a 4th-class red gully
Rockfall onto your own party on the ledges and the slabs below: move one at a time between sheltered stances

2.station: This is the one station on the sequence that is off the fall line — it sits climber's left. Every other station on the face is either straight below the one above it or climber's right, so left is the exception to look for rather than the rule.

6.station: The final station is on your left as you come down toward the last cliff above the snow. Find it before you commit over that edge — it is not on the lip you are walking toward.
hazards: The rappel ends in a moat/bergschrund between the rock and the snowfield rather than on the snow, and its size cannot be judged from the route or from the col on the way in
Parties have had to be lowered into the moat and ice-climb out the far side, or drop into it, traverse a few hundred feet inside, and then cross a steep unstable glacier lip
Reports describe the moat as deep enough that it would have been uncrossable a week later in the season — late-season parties should expect it open
6.pull: Double-rope rappel like the rest of the sequence. Send the first person down carrying a picket, axe and crampons so they can climb out of the moat and protect whoever follows; nobody above can help once the ropes are pulled.

1.station: The first anchor is at your feet on the flat summit area, on the north side — webbing around a chockstone, with a bolt reported at the same spot. Starting the rappel means squeezing down into a small chute directly below the stance.
hazards: That chute has caught pulled ropes more than once; one party freed theirs by loading the strand with a progress-capture device, another had to climb back up for it
1.pull: A single 60 m rope reaches every station on this descent — a second rope adds rope in the chute and more to snag, not more reach.

2.station: Not visible from the summit. You rappel roughly 25 m before it appears, off to climber's left — reported as about 30 ft climber's left and 50 ft downslope of the ledge, on a chockstone jammed between the main wall and a protruding flake. It is a cramped, uncomfortable stance.
hazards: A sling around a small boulder nearer the fall line looks like the station and has been reported as poor; the anchor in use is below it and further to climber's left
Because it is out of sight and off the fall line, this is the station parties overshoot

3.station: Visible immediately below station 2 — once established at 2 you can see where you are going, so no searching.

4.station: Reported relocated into a small alcove climber's left of station 3.
hazards: The alcove sits directly under a large amount of loose rock: the pulled rope can bring it down onto whoever is at the station, and the same broken ground snags ropes

6.station: Rigged near the balanced rock at the base of the West Ridge, dropping down the south side from the notch. It is avoidable — parties who scramble further west reach easy ground without rigging it at all.

1.station: From the heavily slung boulder on the summit the line drops down the middle of the upper face to the only bolted anchor on the entire descent, sitting on a ledge.
hazards: A 60 m rope doubled comes up short of it — you finish about 10 ft above the bolts and have to downclimb easy but unprotected 5th class off the ends to reach them
1.pull: Two ropes or a 70 m if you want to arrive at the bolts on rope. On a single 60 m, plan the downclimb deliberately rather than discovering it at the ends.

2.station: Lands on a large ledge beside the rock arch. The next anchor is not below where you land — walk the ledge across to a constriction where slings back up the station.
hazards: The station is reached by traversing rather than rappelling, so a party looking straight down from the landing will not find an anchor

3.station: The slung constriction above the wide-crack ground; the rappel runs down lichen-covered rock to a horn carrying a blue sling, set climber's right of the ascent line.
hazards: The constriction swallows a pulled rope — one party had to lead back up the ground below it to free theirs
Lichen-covered rock the whole way, and the descent generally has many places for a rope to hang up

4.station: From the blue-slung horn down to the broad, scree-covered upper ledges.
hazards: Genuine potential to snag the rope on the ledge system below — pull from clear of the fall line and watch the strand all the way down

2.station: The highest chockstone in the Great Chimney. There are two ways to rig it: through the low keyhole/tunnel under the chockstone, which is the recommended line and gives a low-angle drop, or over the lip of the chockstone, which is overhanging.
hazards: The tunnel is a real squeeze — packs come off and get pushed through ahead of you, which is exactly why parties take the lip instead
Going over the lip loads the chockstone edge: a block there has split under rope tension and run down the chimney, striking both climbers of one party
Anchors through the chimney are aged natural slings, described by more than one party as questionable, and the chimney funnels everything that comes loose
2.pull: About 75 ft of drop, so a 60 m rope doubled covers it. A party on 25 m ropes was left roughly five metres short and had to break the chimney into two rappels.

3.station: A slung chockstone partway down the chimney. The rappel ends on a narrow, exposed ledge — from there parties traverse back to the high southeast notch rather than continuing straight down the chimney line.
hazards: The landing is a narrow exposed ledge, not easy ground, and it is where the descent changes direction
Anything dislodged in the chimney runs a long way; parties on this face have sent rock all the way down to the glacier below

4.station: Rappel down the snow/rock gully from the high southeast notch. Halfway down the line threads a second cannonhole — this one a hole through a tall snow fin.
hazards: Moats are open on both sides of the snow fin at the hole

5.station: The final rappel drops through a cleft in the rock of the southeast rib back onto walking terrain.
hazards: This is the documented rope-eater on the route: a party's rope jammed on the pull here, resisted every retrieval attempt, and was left on the mountain — in the dark, on the way out
5.pull: Pull from as far out of the cleft as the ground allows, and treat a spare cord or a stuck-rope plan as part of the rack rather than optional.

wa_lincoln_peak_north_ridge.skip_reason: No published account describes a rappel descent of Lincoln Peak's north ridge/north face station by station. The stored five stations are an even 5 x 30 m reconstruction, not a documented station list. What exists is either about a different line on the peak or a bare statement that a party rappelled most of the way down on two 60 m ropes, with no anchor locations, features or lengths. Nothing can be added without inventing it.

wa_big_four_mountain_spindrift_couloir.skip_reason: The published accounts give the descent only in outline — downclimb the northwest ridge to a treed col, rappel from there into the north face bowl, then several more rappels off trees to the base — with no station locations, anchor descriptions, lengths or a count. The stored four stations are already flagged as an approximate reconstruction, so there is no published per-station fact to attach to any of them.

wa_nooksack_tower_south_face.skip_reason: Published descents disagree on both the line and the count: four rappels off natural gear to the col on two 60 m ropes; a single rappel off a stopper and a runner onto a pocket glacier and out a short couloir; and about ten 60 m rappels including one off a buried picket in the upper couloir. None is a station-by-station description, and the stored ten stations are explicitly estimated placeholders, so no published fact maps onto a numbered station here.
